fact: The economy is rigged against working people

framings.framing_headline: The 'rigged economy' narrative is alarmist oversimplification that cherry-picks data and ignores methodological nuance showing real income gains for most Americans
framings.perspective: Pro-market, center-right libertarian/classical liberal; affiliated with Hoover Institution (Stanford), skeptical of progressive economic critique and government intervention narratives
framings.emphasizes: Methodological ambiguity in income inequality studies, income mobility data, CBO findings showing 37-57% median income growth, fluidity of income classes, dangers of political radicalization driven by overstated economic pessimism
framings.downplays: The structural barriers that concentrate wealth, the lived experience of wage stagnation for low-income workers, the validity of Stiglitz's core finding that top earners have captured disproportionate gains, and the policy implications of persistent relative immobility
framings.who_benefits: Pro-market conservatives, free-market think tanks, opponents of redistributive economic policy, and those who prefer incremental rather than structural reform of the economy
framings.excerpt: Maybe the economy and public policy are not so rigged after all. The gloomiest studies take a snapshot of the income distribution at a point in time and compare to one in the past. But the people in the snapshots are not the same.

framings.framing_headline: Inequality is not an accident but the deliberate result of policy choices designed to enrich those already at the top at workers' expense
framings.perspective: Progressive-left, heterodox economist perspective; structural critique of capitalism focused on policy-driven inequality and rent extraction by elites
framings.emphasizes: Conscious policy design as the root cause of upward income redistribution; specific mechanisms (trade rules, patents, copyrights, corporate governance, macroeconomic policy) that transfer wealth upward; the idea that markets are not 'free' but rigged by powerful interests; actionable reform agenda
framings.downplays: Any role of neutral market forces, technological change, or skills-based explanations for inequality; potential trade-offs or costs of proposed reforms; perspectives that attribute inequality to factors other than deliberate elite manipulation
framings.who_benefits: Working and middle-class readers seeking a structural explanation for their economic stagnation; progressive policymakers looking for an intellectual framework; labor advocates and left-leaning economists
framings.excerpt: Baker shows that this upward redistribution was not the result of globalization and the natural workings of the market. Rather it was the result of conscious policies that were designed to put downward pressure on the wages of ordinary workers while protecting and enhancing the incomes of those at the top.

framings.framing_headline: Nobel economist Stiglitz uses academic authority to argue systemic inequality is policy-driven and worsened by Trump-era plutocracy
framings.perspective: progressive academic-institutional; center-left economic reform perspective rooted in mainstream heterodox economics
framings.emphasizes: policy choices as root cause of inequality, the betrayal of the American Dream, statistical comparisons showing US exceptionalism in negative metrics, inherited plutocracy including Trump as the rigging agent, and the quadrupling of top 0.1% income share
framings.downplays: market-based explanations or technological determinism (explicitly dismisses them), potential conservative or libertarian interpretations of inequality data, international trade-offs or complexity in globalization effects
framings.who_benefits: progressive policy advocates, labor-aligned economists, Democratic-leaning reformers, academic institutions seeking policy influence; frames working people as victims of identifiable elite actors
framings.excerpt: President Donald Trump was right in saying that the system is rigged—by those in the inherited plutocracy of which he himself is a member. And he is making it much, much worse.

framings.framing_headline: The American economy is structurally rigged against working people through tax codes, education inequality, and inherited privilege that amount to a new feudalism
framings.perspective: Progressive-populist, with a reformist establishment flavor — authored by mainstream journalists (NYT correspondents) advocating systemic structural change while speaking from a position of acknowledged privilege
framings.emphasizes: Concrete examples of upward wealth transfer (tax loopholes, corporate subsidies, private jet subsidies), education as an inequality machine, racial disparities, feudalism analogy, and the hypocrisy of affluent liberals
framings.downplays: Market-based solutions, individual agency, economic mobility success stories, any counterarguments about meritocracy functioning in some sectors, or the role of global economic forces versus domestic policy choices
framings.who_benefits: Working-class and middle-class readers seeking validation of their economic grievances; progressive policy advocates pushing tax reform and education equity; the authors promoting their book
framings.excerpt: As in historic feudalism, the paramount need is not just for redistribution of income within an unfair system, but for a restructuring of the rules to create a more just society and greater opportunity for those below.

framings.framing_headline: Structural barriers and policy failures—not individual shortcomings—explain why economic mobility has declined and the economy disadvantages working people
framings.perspective: Progressive think-tank, evidence-based policy reform lens focused on structural inequality, racial equity, and gender equity; institutionally aligned with center-left economic policy advocacy
framings.emphasizes: Structural causes of immobility (regressive tax policy, residential segregation, systemic racism, gender bias, intergenerational wealth transfers), racial and gender disparities in mobility, the Great Gatsby Curve linking inequality to low mobility, and policy interventions like tax reform and social infrastructure investment
framings.downplays: Individual agency and market-based solutions, the role of cultural or behavioral factors, any evidence that the system produces broadly positive outcomes, and the complexity of policy tradeoffs involved in proposed reforms
framings.who_benefits: Progressive policymakers, labor advocates, racial and gender equity advocates, and researchers seeking evidence-based justification for redistributive policy; the implied audience is policy professionals, academics, and engaged citizens sympathetic to structural explanations of inequality
framings.excerpt: Low levels of economic and social mobility across generations are largely due to structural issues, which limit opportunity and keep economic statuses in place over generations.

framings.framing_headline: The economy is rigged not because meritocracy is flawed, but because we have failed to implement a truly fair meritocracy — the solution is reform, not rejection
framings.perspective: Centrist, pro-meritocracy, reform-minded liberal; defends market capitalism and Enlightenment ideals while acknowledging structural inequality as a correctable dysfunction rather than a systemic feature
framings.emphasizes: The ideal of meritocracy as inherently just and worth preserving, the education gap as the primary mechanism of economic unfairness, the need for equal opportunity reform rather than systemic overhaul, and sports/American dream optimism as a civic framework
framings.downplays: Class power dynamics, labor exploitation, corporate lobbying influence on wages, the possibility that meritocracy itself legitimizes inequality, and structural critiques that go beyond education access
framings.who_benefits: Centrist reformers, pro-market liberals, education policy advocates, and business-aligned civic organizations; audiences who want to acknowledge inequality without challenging capitalism's foundational legitimacy
framings.excerpt: This game is rigged in favor of those market participants who have been permitted to leverage their economic power to wield political power... it is not the concept of meritocracy that is the problem, but its present-day execution.

framings.framing_headline: Declining social mobility is a solvable policy problem, not a systemic injustice, according to data-driven academic research
framings.perspective: Technocratic, evidence-based, elite academic institutionalism — reform-oriented but operating within existing systems
framings.emphasizes: Data-driven diagnosis of mobility decline, neighborhood-level determinants of economic outcomes, cost-effective policy interventions, the role of universities and research institutions in guiding reform
framings.downplays: Structural power imbalances, corporate influence on wages and policy, wealth concentration at the top, systemic exploitation — the 'rigging' framing is entirely absent
framings.who_benefits: Policymakers, university institutions, researchers, and philanthropic reformers who favor incremental evidence-based interventions over structural redistribution or systemic critique
framings.excerpt: It is this very trend that underlies a lot of the frustration that people around the U.S. are expressing, that this is no longer a country where it's easy to get ahead, even through hard work.

framings.framing_headline: The Federal Reserve frames low intergenerational mobility as an empirical research finding requiring evidence-based policy solutions, not as systemic rigging
framings.perspective: Technocratic, institutionalist, data-driven; Federal Reserve establishment perspective that treats inequality as a measurable policy problem rather than a moral or political failing
framings.emphasizes: Methodological evolution in measuring mobility, racial disparities in upward/downward mobility, international comparisons showing U.S. underperformance, the Great Gatsby Curve correlation between inequality and low mobility
framings.downplays: Power dynamics, deliberate policy choices that created inequality, corporate or elite agency in maintaining an unequal system, the normative claim that the economy is 'rigged' — language of structural injustice is replaced with neutral statistical language
framings.who_benefits: Policymakers and academics who prefer technocratic solutions over structural or political critique; the framing avoids blame and keeps solutions within mainstream institutional channels
framings.excerpt: the new evidence suggested that, rather than being a country with relatively high mobility, the U.S. was actually a relatively rigid society in which income gaps were likely to persist for many generations
